translationRepairs: In the thirty-second year of Kangxi, Russia again sent the envoy Nicolis Spafari to court; the emperor received him in audience for the first time and granted seated reception and food.
In the thirty-second year of Kangxi, Russia again sent the envoy Izbrant Ides to court; the emperor received him in audience for the first time and granted seated reception and food.

s0075 names the Kangxi-32 Russian envoy 義茲柏阿朗迭義迭, a phonetic form of Izbrant/Ysbrants Ides, not Nicolis Spafari. The proposed idiomatic corrects that misidentification while leaving the rest of the sentence intact.
In the thirty-second year of Kangxi, Russia again sent the envoy Nicolis Spafari to court; the emperor received him in audience for the first time and granted seated reception and food.
In the thirty-second year of Kangxi, Russia again sent the envoy Izbrant Ides to court; the emperor received him in audience for the first time and granted seated reception and food.
The literal of s0075 likewise replaces Spafari with a name matching 義茲柏阿朗迭義迭; Izbrant Ides is the supported rendering.

Your humble subject Yangbu, though far from the capital and still young, humbly entreats that when I serve among the attendants, you will kindly instruct me, for the grace would not be slight," and so forth.

Your humble subject's seat at Yangbu is far from the capital, and [I am] still young; [I] humbly entreat that when I serve among the attendants, you will kindly instruct me, for the grace would not be slight," and so forth.

In s0092, 小臣陽布離京遠 treats 陽布 as the speaker's seat (Kathmandu), not as a personal name; the before text wrongly apposes Yangbu to "humble subject." The proposed after restores the place reading but is ungrammatical ("seat … humbly entreats"). Revise to keep Yangbu as place and supply a finite first-person verb.

In the twenty-first year, England again sent envoys to present tribute; the officials told them they must perform the kneeling and kowtowing rites; Lord Amherst and others then claimed illness and refused audience; the emperor in anger ordered them sent home and canceled the banquet and gifts.

In the twenty-first year, England again sent envoys to present tribute; the officials told them they must perform the kneeling and kowtowing rites; Staunton and others then claimed illness and refused audience; the emperor in anger ordered them sent home and canceled the banquet and gifts.
s0094's named figure is 司當冬, which matches Staunton; Lord Amherst would be written 阿美士德. The idiomatic correctly substitutes Staunton for the invented Amherst reading.

In the twenty-first year, England again sent envoys to present tribute; the officials told them they must perform the kneeling and kowtowing rites; Lord Amherst and others then claimed illness and refused audience; the emperor in anger ordered them sent home and canceled the banquet and gifts.

In the twenty-first year, England again sent envoys to present tribute; the officials told them they must perform the kneeling and kowtowing rites; Staunton and others then claimed illness and refused audience; the emperor in anger ordered them sent home and canceled the banquet and gifts.
The literal must likewise render 司當冬 as Staunton rather than Lord Amherst; the proposed replacement matches the Chinese name.

That summer, the Japanese envoy Soejima Taneomi, the Russian envoy Yariga, the American envoy Frederick Low, the English envoy Thomas Wade, the French envoy Revell, and the Dutch envoy Vigoonsen were received in audience at the Ziguang Pavilion, presented their credentials, and followed the agreed commercial protocol.

That summer, the Japanese envoy Soejima Taneomi, the Russian envoy Vlangaly, the American envoy Frederick Low, the English envoy Thomas Wade, the French envoy Revell, and the Dutch envoy Vigoonsen were received in audience at the Ziguang Pavilion, presented their credentials, and followed the agreed commercial protocol.
s0162 lists 俄使臣倭良嘎哩; 倭良嘎哩 is the established Chinese form of the Russian minister Vlangaly/Vlangali, not "Yariga." The proposed idiomatic corrects only that name.

That day at the si hour, the emperor held court at the Hall of Jade Ripples; Prince Henry entered together with the German envoy Heinrich von Heiden and others; officials of the foreign ministry led them in through the east side gate of the hall to rest briefly in the canvas tent.

That day at the si hour, the emperor held court at the Hall of Jade Ripples; Prince Henry entered together with the German envoy Heyking and others; officials of the foreign ministry led them in through the east side gate of the hall to rest briefly in the canvas tent.
s0193 has 德使海靖; 海靖 is the German minister Heyking (von Heyking), not Heinrich von Heiden. The proposed idiomatic restores the correct name.

That day at the si hour, the emperor held court at the Hall of Jade Ripples; Prince Henry entered together with the German envoy Heinrich von Heiden and others; officials of the foreign ministry led them in through the east side gate of the hall to rest briefly in the canvas tent.

That day at the si hour, the emperor held court at the Hall of Jade Ripples; Prince Henry entered together with the German envoy Heyking and others; officials of the foreign ministry led them in through the east side gate of the hall to rest briefly in the canvas tent.
The literal of s0193 likewise misreads 海靖 as Heinrich von Heiden; Heyking matches the Chinese form.

When subordinate officials of the Grand Secretariat, ministries, directorates, and superintendent offices called on their superiors for a first meeting, they went to the office in official dress, ascended by the eastern steps, presented their calling cards and arranged their seat mats, and bowed with joined hands three times facing one another in order; the superior left his seat to return the bows.

When subordinate officials of the Grand Secretariat, ministries, directorates, and superintendent offices called on their superiors for a first meeting, they went to the office in official dress, ascended by the eastern steps, presented their service records and arranged their seat mats, and bowed with joined hands three times facing one another in order; the superior left his seat to return the bows.
s0252 reads 具履行陳坐案: 履行 is service/career records (as in s0303), and this unit has no 名柬. "Calling cards" invents content; "service records" is accurate.

When subordinate officials of the Grand Secretariat, ministries, directorates, and superintendent offices called on their superiors for a first meeting, wearing official dress they went to the office, ascended by the eastern steps, presented their calling cards and arranged their seat mats, bowed with hands joined three times facing each other in order, and the superior left his seat to return the bows.

When subordinate officials of the Grand Secretariat, ministries, directorates, and superintendent offices called on their superiors for a first meeting, wearing official dress they went to the office, ascended by the eastern steps, presented their service records and arranged their seat mats, bowed with hands joined three times facing each other in order, and the superior left his seat to return the bows.
The literal likewise mistranslates 具履行 as calling cards; replacing with service records aligns with the Chinese and with 履行 in s0303.

On a first meeting they presented a calling card bearing their name and took their place on the mat. When civil intendants called on governors-general or governors, the host welcomed them inside the screen behind the hall.

On a first meeting they presented a calling card bearing their name and submitted their service records. When civil intendants called on governors-general or governors, the host welcomed them inside the screen behind the hall.
s0274 has 初見具名柬，呈履行: name cards and submitting 履行 (service records) are separate acts. "Took their place on the mat" invents seating for 呈履行; the proposed idiomatic restores both elements.

On a first meeting they presented a calling card bearing their name and took their place on the mat; when civil intendants called on governors-general or governors, the host welcomed them inside the screen behind the hall.

On a first meeting they presented a calling card bearing their name and submitted their service records; when civil intendants called on governors-general or governors, the host welcomed them inside the screen behind the hall.
The literal must also render 呈履行 as submitting service records rather than seating on a mat, while keeping 具名柬 as the calling card.
Transport officials and assistant prefects ranked below them in turn.
Transport deputies and assistant commissioners followed in descending order of rank.

After 運使 in s0301, s0302's 運、判 continues the salt-transport ladder (運同/運副 and 運判). "Assistant prefects" misreads 判 as 通判; "transport deputies and assistant commissioners" matches the hierarchy and 以次遞降.
Transport officials and assistant prefects followed in descending order of rank.
Transport deputies and assistant commissioners followed in descending order of rank.
The literal likewise wrongly takes 判 as assistant prefect; in context after 運使, 運、判 are salt-transport subordinate ranks, correctly rendered as transport deputies and assistant commissioners.
